content.title: Gay Vanderbilt coach Kevin DeMille wins award during Sweet 16 - Outsports
content.text: There are a few inspiring LGBTQ coaches remaining in the women’s March Madness tournament heading into the Sweet 16. Kevin DeMille, an assistant coach for the Vanderbilt Commodores women’s basketball team, is adding a solo accomplishment to his resume heading into the second week of March Madness. DeMille was just honored with the Women’s Basketball Coaches Association (WBCA) Assistant Coach of the Year award. His leadership has been instrumental in helping Vandy win 29 games so far this season, and the program is in its first Sweet 16 since 2009. The team congratulated DeMille on Instagram when he won the accolade. Get off the sidelines and into the game Our weekly newsletter is packed with everything from locker room chatter to pressing LGBTQ sports issues. DeMille’s rise within women’s college hoops hasn’t happened overnight. It’s been a gradual list of small accomplishments that keep growing in stature every year. We’ve been so happy here at Outsports to support every step in his career as one of basketball’s leading LGBTQ advocates. DeMille was on the Commodores’ coaching staff when they went to the NCAA Tournament for the first time in a decade back in 2024. He previously worked on the coaching staffs for George Washington as well as UConn, the most successful women’s college basketball program ever. DeMille living his life openly while still growing his career on the court is proof that LGBTQ athletes and coaches can show their true selves and also succeed at the highest level. DeMille always puts his trail-blazing lifestyle in perspective so that others can live out and proud lives in athletics. In June 2022, DeMille wrote an essay on the relevance of celebrating Pride and how his personal journey to self-acceptance has evolved throughout his life and career. “We deserve to celebrate our identities and what makes us us. We also deserve to feel like our love, our relationships, our families and our lives are equal … and normal. It takes a lot of courage, confidence and support to come out, and too few of us get to do that safely. Therefore, those of us who can do it safely have a responsibility to make it safer for others.” “As a visible gay person, I have a responsibility to show others in the community that they belong and are welcome in all spaces, and I have a responsibility to normalize the concept of gay men and LGBTQ+ people coaching college sports.” Normalizing being gay in college sports and athletics in general is vital to more LGBTQ individuals coming out. As those in the closet feel afraid to come out, maybe seeing someone like DeMille not only coach successfully, but also win awards that recognize his career, will show the world that being gay and succeeding in traditionally heteronormative spaces is possible.
